blocks.text: A drone manufacturer needs a boom arm that stays stiff, survives a hot parked vehicle and costs under a set limit per kilogram. A database lists hundreds of materials: no engineer reads them all. Screening throws out the impossible ones, an index ranks what is left, and a chart makes the ranking visible at a glance.

blocks.markdown: Once a performance index has been derived (for a stiff, light beam of square section it is $M=E^{1/2}/\rho$), the work of selection is mechanical. It runs in three stages: **screen** with pass/fail constraints, **rank** the survivors with the index, and then **resolve** any conflict between performance and cost with an explicit trade-off value. This unit shows each stage with numbers.

blocks.title: Screening, ranking and the exchange constant
blocks.text: **Screening** removes every material that fails a hard limit (for example $E\ge E_{\min}$, maximum service temperature, cost per kilogram). **Ranking** orders the survivors by the performance index $M$. The **exchange constant** $\alpha$ is the value, in USD per kg, that the designer places on saving one kilogram of mass.

blocks.caption: Candidate set used in this unit. Values are typical and rounded; cost is an illustrative price. The index is in GPa^(1/2) per (Mg/m^3).

blocks.title: Screen then rank a drone boom arm
blocks.prompt: A boom arm must have $E\ge30$ GPa, cost at most USD 20 per kg and survive 100 C. Every material in the table passes the temperature limit. Screen the table and rank the survivors by $M=E^{1/2}/\rho$ (E in GPa, $\rho$ in Mg m$^{-3}$).

steps.text: Apply the stiffness limit $E\ge30$ GPa. GFRP has $E=20$ GPa and is removed; all other materials pass.
Apply the cost limit of USD 20 per kg. Ti-6Al-4V (45) and CFRP (60) are removed. Survivors: steel, aluminium alloy, magnesium alloy.
Compute the index for each survivor.
Rank by index: higher $M$ means lower mass for the required stiffness. The magnesium alloy ranks first, aluminium second, steel last.

blocks.answer: Magnesium alloy (M = 3.79), then aluminium alloy (3.08), then steel (1.85); GFRP, titanium and CFRP are screened out.

blocks.markdown: **Property charts and selection lines.** On a chart of $\log E$ against $\log\rho$, every material is a point. Because $M=E^{1/2}/\rho$, a given value $M_0$ satisfies $\log E=2\log\rho+2\log M_0$, which is a straight line of **slope 2**. Moving the line upward raises $M_0$. All materials on or above the line have $M\ge M_0$; those below it are worse. For a different index $M=E^{1/n}/\rho$ the line has slope $n$ (slope 3 for a stiff light panel, $E^{1/3}/\rho$).

blocks.latex: M=\frac{E^{1/2}}{\rho}\ \Rightarrow\ \log E=2\log\rho+2\log M_0\qquad\text{(slope 2 on a log-log chart)}
blocks.caption: Selection line for the index E^(1/2)/rho; materials above the line have an index larger than M0.

blocks.title: Place a selection line on the chart
blocks.prompt: Draw the line $M_0=3.0$ GPa$^{1/2}$/(Mg m$^{-3}$) through the candidate set and decide which of steel, aluminium alloy and magnesium alloy lie above it.

steps.text: Write the line equation in linear form.
Evaluate the line at each density. At $\rho=2.70$ the line sits at $E=65.6$ GPa, at $\rho=7.85$ at $E=555$ GPa and at $\rho=1.77$ at $E=28.2$ GPa.
Compare each material's actual modulus with the line value at its own density. Aluminium (69 > 65.6) and magnesium (45 > 28.2) lie above the line; steel (210 < 555) lies far below it.
Aluminium and magnesium therefore satisfy $M\ge3.0$; steel does not, in agreement with the indices 3.08, 3.79 and 1.85.

blocks.answer: The selection line at M0 = 3.0 separates aluminium and magnesium (above) from steel (below).

blocks.markdown: **Trade-offs.** Performance and cost often conflict: the lightest material is rarely the cheapest. A single combined objective turns this into a ranking. If the mass required is $m=k/M$ (with $k$ set by the geometry and load, the same for all materials), the cost of material is $C\,m$ ($C$ in USD/kg) and each kilogram of mass is valued at $\alpha$, the combined cost is $Z=(C+\alpha)\,m$. Minimising $Z$ means minimising $(C+\alpha)/M$.

blocks.caption: C is the material price in USD per kg, alpha the value of a kilogram saved in USD per kg, and M the performance index.

blocks.title: Resolve a cost conflict at two exchange constants
blocks.prompt: Using the table, find the best material for the stiff beam when $\alpha=0$ (cost only) and when $\alpha=100$ USD/kg (a weight-critical aircraft), with no cost limit. Then find the exchange constant at which aluminium alloy overtakes steel.

steps.text: Cost only ($\alpha=0$): evaluate $C/M$. Steel is $1/1.85=0.54$, aluminium $0.98$, magnesium $1.06$, GFRP $1.70$, CFRP $9.3$, titanium $18.7$. Steel is cheapest per unit of performance.
Weight-critical ($\alpha=100$): evaluate $(C+100)/M$. Steel $54.7$, aluminium $33.5$, magnesium $27.4$, GFRP $44.2$, titanium $60.2$, CFRP $24.8$. CFRP now wins despite its price.
For the aluminium/steel crossover set the two costs equal and solve for $\alpha$.

blocks.answer: Steel wins at alpha = 0, CFRP wins at alpha = 100 USD/kg, and aluminium overtakes steel above alpha of about 2 USD/kg.

headers: Exchange constant alpha (USD per kg saved)
rows: Cheapest material that meets the constraints
Lowest mass at almost any price
blocks.caption: Higher alpha pushes the choice toward lighter and more expensive materials.

blocks.title: Screen before you rank
blocks.text: A material that fails a hard constraint (temperature, toughness, cost limit) must be removed even if it has the highest index; the index only ranks materials that are already acceptable. Also, indices rank under the stated shape and loading assumptions: change the geometry and the ranking can change.

points: Screening applies pass/fail limits first; the performance index then ranks the survivors, and a higher index means less mass for the same function.
For $M=E^{1/n}/\rho$ the selection line on a log $E$ against log $\rho$ chart has slope $n$ (slope 2 for $E^{1/2}/\rho$); materials above the line have a larger index.
Cost and performance conflicts are resolved by minimising $(C+\alpha)/M$, where the exchange constant $\alpha$ is the value of saving 1 kg; higher $\alpha$ favours lighter, costlier materials.

questions.stem: A candidate material has the highest performance index in the database but its maximum service temperature is below the operating temperature. What should the selection procedure do?

options.text: Keep it, because the index is the only criterion that matters
Keep it but halve its index to account for the temperature
Eliminate it at the screening stage, because the temperature limit is a pass/fail constraint
Rank it last among the survivors and accept the risk

questions.correctOptionText: Eliminate it at the screening stage, because the temperature limit is a pass/fail constraint

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: the index only ranks materials that already satisfy every constraint.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: there is no rule for halving an index; a constraint is pass or fail.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: constraints are applied first, and a failure removes the material whatever its index.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: ranking last still lets an unsuitable material remain a candidate.

questions.explanation: A limit such as maximum service temperature is a hard constraint, so a material that fails it is removed before ranking. The performance index only orders materials that have already passed every constraint.

questions.stem: A timber has $E=12$ GPa and density $600$ kg m$^{-3}$. Evaluate the beam index $M=E^{1/2}/\rho$ with $E$ in GPa and $\rho$ in Mg m$^{-3}$. Give your answer in GPa$^{1/2}$ per (Mg m$^{-3}$).
questions.explanation: Convert the density to $0.600$ Mg m$^{-3}$ and take $E^{1/2}=\sqrt{12}=3.464$. Then $M=3.464/0.600=5.77$, which is high because the density is very low.

questions.stem: A light stiff panel has the performance index $M=E^{1/3}/\rho$. What is the slope of the selection line on a chart of $\log E$ (vertical) against $\log\rho$ (horizontal)?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: $\log E=3\log\rho+3\log M_0$, so the slope is 3.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: 1/3 is the exponent on E in the index, not the slope; the line must be solved for log E.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: slope 2 belongs to the beam index $E^{1/2}/\rho$.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: a slope of 1 corresponds to the specific stiffness index $E/\rho$.

questions.explanation: Taking logarithms of $M_0=E^{1/3}/\rho$ gives $\tfrac13\log E-\log\rho=\log M_0$, so $\log E=3\log\rho+3\log M_0$. The slope is the reciprocal of the exponent on E, which is 3.

questions.stem: On a $\log E$ against $\log\rho$ chart, a selection line for the beam index $M_0=4$ GPa$^{1/2}$/(Mg m$^{-3}$) passes through $E=16\rho^{2}$. A material has $E=60$ GPa and $\rho=1.8$ Mg m$^{-3}$. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It lies below the line and its index is less than 4
It lies on the line, so its index is exactly 4
It lies above the line but its index is less than 4
It lies above the line and its index is about 4.3, greater than 4

questions.correctOptionText: It lies above the line and its index is about 4.3, greater than 4

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: 60 GPa exceeds the line value, so it lies above, not below.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: the line value 51.8 GPa is not equal to 60 GPa.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: being above the line means a larger index, not a smaller one.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: at $\rho=1.8$ the line sits at $E=51.8$ GPa, the material has 60 GPa, and $\sqrt{60}/1.8=4.30$.

questions.explanation: The line value at $\rho=1.8$ is $16\times1.8^{2}=51.8$ GPa, which is below the material's 60 GPa, so the point is above the line. Directly, $M=\sqrt{60}/1.8=4.30>4$, which confirms that points above the line have the larger index.

questions.stem: A selection line for $M_0=3.5$ GPa$^{1/2}$/(Mg m$^{-3}$) is drawn on a log-log chart of $E$ against $\rho$. What modulus, in GPa, does the line have at $\rho=2.0$ Mg m$^{-3}$?
questions.explanation: The line satisfies $E=(M_0\rho)^2$. At $\rho=2.0$ this is $(3.5\times2.0)^2=7.0^{2}=49$ GPa, so a material at this density needs a modulus of at least 49 GPa to be on or above the line.

questions.stem: Two materials give the same stiffness for the same geometry. Material P has price USD 2.0 per kg and index $M=2.5$; Material Q has price USD 14 per kg and index $M=5.0$ (same units). Find the exchange constant $\alpha$, in USD per kg, at which the two have equal combined cost $Z\propto(C+\alpha)/M$.
questions.explanation: Set $(2+\alpha)/2.5=(14+\alpha)/5.0$, so $5(2+\alpha)=2.5(14+\alpha)$, giving $10+5\alpha=35+2.5\alpha$. Then $2.5\alpha=25$ and $\alpha=10$ USD/kg; for larger $\alpha$ the lighter, dearer material Q is better.

questions.stem: Material R costs USD 5 per kg with index $M=3.0$; material S costs USD 25 per kg with index $M=4.5$. For a weight-critical application the exchange constant is $\alpha=60$ USD/kg. Using $Z\propto(C+\alpha)/M$, which material should be chosen?

options.text: Material R, because it has the lower price per kilogram
Material S, because $(25+60)/4.5=18.9$ is lower than $(5+60)/3.0=21.7$
Material R, because its combined value $(5+60)/3.0=21.7$ is lower than that of S
Material S, because it has the higher price and so must be better

questions.correctOptionText: Material S, because $(25+60)/4.5=18.9$ is lower than $(5+60)/3.0=21.7$

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: price per kilogram alone ignores the extra mass of the poorer material.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: the combined cost is lower for S once the value of mass is counted.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: 21.7 is larger than 18.9, so R has the higher combined cost.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: price is not a measure of performance; the choice follows from the numbers.

questions.explanation: At $\alpha=60$ the combined measure is $(5+60)/3.0=21.7$ for R and $(25+60)/4.5=18.9$ for S, so S is better. The crossover is at $\alpha=35$ USD/kg, since $(5+35)/3.0=(25+35)/4.5$, so a mass-critical application above that value favours S.

questions.stem: A beam must be stiff and light and a screen needs at least $T_{\max}\ge120$ C and price at most USD 10 per kg. Five candidates are listed as (E in GPa, $\rho$ in Mg m$^{-3}$, $T_{\max}$ in C, price in USD/kg): A (70, 2.7, 200, 3.0); B (45, 1.8, 100, 4.0); C (110, 4.4, 400, 30); D (200, 7.8, 500, 1.0); E (38, 1.4, 150, 8.0). Which is the best choice by $E^{1/2}/\rho$ after screening?

options.text: B, with an index of about 3.7
A, with an index of about 3.1
D, with an index of about 1.8
E, with an index of about 4.4

questions.correctOptionText: E, with an index of about 4.4

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: B has a high index but fails the 120 C limit.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: A passes the screen, but its index of 3.1 is below that of the correct material.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: D passes but has the lowest index of the survivors.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: E passes both limits (150 C, 8 USD per kg) and has the largest index among the survivors A, D and E.

questions.explanation: B fails the temperature limit (100 C) and C fails the price limit (30 USD per kg), so A, D and E survive. Their indices are $\sqrt{70}/2.7=3.10$, $\sqrt{200}/7.8=1.81$ and $\sqrt{38}/1.4=4.40$, so E ranks first.

questions.stem: Describe, in order, how a designer selects a material for a lightweight stiff beam from a database of 3000 materials using screening, ranking and a chart. Explain what the selection line represents and why a material above it is preferred.
markingGuide: Screening: apply pass/fail constraints (for example minimum modulus, service temperature, price) to remove unsuitable materials
Ranking: compute the performance index (here $E^{1/2}/\rho$) for survivors and order them, larger index meaning less mass
Chart: plot $\log E$ against $\log\rho$; the line $\log E=2\log\rho+2\log M_0$ has slope 2 and represents constant index $M_0$
Materials above the line have a larger index, so lower mass for the same stiffness; moving the line up tightens the selection
States that the survivors are then checked against secondary criteria (cost, manufacturability, other constraints)
questions.explanation: Selection proceeds from hard constraints to an index-based ranking and then to a visual check. The line on the chart is a graphical statement of the index, so everything above it beats the chosen threshold.

questions.stem: A weight-critical aerospace bracket and a low-cost domestic appliance bracket need the same stiffness. Explain, using the exchange constant $\alpha$ and the combined cost $Z\propto(C+\alpha)/M$, why they may end up using different materials, and describe what happens to the best choice as $\alpha$ increases.
markingGuide: Defines alpha as the value (in USD per kg) of saving one kilogram of mass
Writes the combined cost as proportional to $(C+\alpha)/M$, with C the price per kg and M the performance index
For the appliance alpha is near zero, so the lowest $C/M$ (cheap, heavy material) wins
For the aerospace bracket alpha is large, so the $\alpha$ term dominates and the choice follows the largest M (light, costly material)
As alpha increases the optimum moves from cheap, low-index materials to expensive, high-index ones, with crossover values found by equating the two $(C+\alpha)/M$ expressions
questions.explanation: The exchange constant decides how much a kilogram is worth, so the same index and price data give different optimal materials in different industries. Large alpha makes the term in $C$ negligible, whereas small alpha makes price the dominant term.
